data.title: He Yi: Crypto needs to return to common business sense; Binance needs to return to seeking truth and being pragmatic.
data.description:
Author: KarenZ, Foresight News

During Binance Blockchain Week 2026, Binance co-founder He Yi gave a group interview to several media outlets, sharing her insights on topics such as security defense in the AI ​​era, organizational and talent transformation, stock tokenization, the positioning of Binance Alpha, challenges facing the crypto industry, global compliance progress, and Binance's competition over the next decade.

The following are the key information and viewpoints from this group interview:

  • Security Defense: Previously, Binance had issues with overly lenient AI permission settings when promoting AI use among employees. Currently, Binance is strengthening its security system from aspects such as employee security awareness, technical means, and sandbox environment, and has hired three external security auditing firms.

AI and Organizational Change: Binance initially attempted to apply AI to its customer service operations, but after a year, the results were minimal. Later, through data cleaning, structuring, and model training, it gradually achieved success. Binance's talent requirements have changed, and it is also considering whether to leverage AI to merge some job functions and change its past hierarchical, assembly-line organizational structure. In departments where AI applications are relatively mature, Binance has neither significantly increased recruitment nor significantly reduced staff. Stock Tokenization: Binance is revamping its stock business liquidity mechanism and expects to soon be able to directly access the liquidity of traditional brokerages. Furthermore, Binance is discussing with several exchanges the possibility of tokenizing stocks from the first day of listing. **Industry Challenges:** The biggest problem in the current crypto industry is "asset hollowing out," not a lack of new narratives. Good tokens should be built on business models with cash flow, revenue, and profit. Ultimately, the industry must return to common business sense, rather than constantly chasing new narratives. A crucial responsibility of exchanges is maintaining ecosystem balance. **Market and Investment:** While believing in market cycles and value investing, based on professional characteristics, liquidity is considered the primary factor. **Global Compliance:** Binance is communicating simultaneously with regulatory agencies in hundreds of countries, prioritizing populous and economically developed markets. As the industry becomes more mainstream, increased regulatory requirements and compliance costs are normal.

  • Competition in the Next Decade: In response to Foresight News' question, "What is most likely to defeat Binance in the next decade?", He Yi believes it's something new that hasn't yet emerged. However, from an organizational development perspective, the biggest threat always comes from within. She mentioned that in the past two years, Binance has placed greater emphasis on "objectivity" and "fairness," and considers curiosity, proactive learning ability, and a sense of ownership as important factors in observing whether a team continues to grow.

    • The following is a transcript of the group interview, with some colloquial expressions and repetitive content removed without changing the original meaning.

    Security Defense and Organizational Change in the AI ​​Era

    Question: Facing new AI-driven attacks, what practical experience and defense strategies can Binance share?

    He Yi: First, objectively speaking, **after the incident in 2019, our company's security facilities were implemented according to the Zero Trust principle, with strict isolation between departments. This is why we haven't had any security problems for so many years.** From an external perspective, people might simply look at the whole incident. But social engineering attacks happen every day, and some real-life incidents are even more outrageous and insane than people imagine.** For example, someone comes for an interview, and the entire interview process is conducted by one person, but when they finally report for duty and onboard, they become a different person. However, during onboarding, we find that this person doesn't match, so we disconnect them. In other cases, before they even enter the system, if you directly ask them, that person simply disappears.** But I think there is indeed a problem this time. Because we were also promoting the use of AI, our AI permission settings weren't strict enough at the time; AI permissions became too lenient. AI is indeed a remarkable weapon, but it also brings risks. Previously, we required exams, such as training followed by testing. However, this time it's not just simple training, but company-wide training, and we've also hired third-party organizations. We've been doing this for the past month. If any related violations occur again, the employee may be immediately dismissed. From an employee awareness perspective, we need to make them understand that they may be facing real social engineering attacks every day. Second, we've now established a sandbox environment where everyone uses company equipment. Third, we're rethinking the internal data boundaries in the AI ​​usage process. Besides having AI write code, we'll also have another AI to monitor the information uploaded daily. Instead of a single AI handling uploading, downloading, and monitoring simultaneously, a dedicated AI for security auditing provides 24/7 oversight. From employee awareness to technical measures and the sandbox environment, this is the foundational security system we are rebuilding. My current requirement for them is, **the overarching principle is to minimize permissions and information access**. Because we've been working remotely since 2019, many people may have grasped the concept, but their execution hasn't been meticulous enough. Therefore, we can't just be aware of this; we need to use strong measures to control it. We've always respected our employees, but freedom comes with responsibility. In the past, we gave employees considerable freedom, especially regarding security permissions. Currently, we have hired three external security auditing firms. Question: What specific product rules or performance indicators does Binance have to ensure user interests are prioritized? How does it balance commercial revenue and user interests? He Yi: An English media outlet asked a similar question before, asking if Binance's revenue would increase in five years. My view is that every industry has its so-called growth period and boom period. During the growth and boom periods, your profits and revenue will naturally be higher, but when the industry matures, the situation will be different. Essentially, I believe Binance is not pursuing pure profit, but rather what core value it provides to users and the public. When you generate a strong enough network effect, even if you only charge a small amount, if you have a large enough user base, you can still generate economies of scale.

    Many of our users in various countries and regions are not typical trading users. This might be different from what you imagine. You might think they're all just speculating on cryptocurrencies or gambling, but unfortunately, our users are incredibly diverse, encompassing all sorts of types.

    For example, in one country, they basically use Binance like Alipay, integrating it into their daily lives.

    In other countries, such as the Philippines, where many people work abroad, and including Pakistan, a common use case is sending money home.

    In these real-world scenarios, you're not comparing which crypto platform has the lowest fees; your competitor is traditional international money exchange services, and you're comparing exchange rates.

    So why is revenue important? Because you still need a healthy business model. But is revenue the most important thing? No. Ultimately, it's about what value the company can provide to its users.

    Of course, when you segment all users, some users live in countries with high inflation rates and need a place to store their money or invest. The needs of these users are different. Question: As AI Agents begin to enter financial scenarios such as payments and transactions, how should exchanges view AI Agents? What is Binance's most important responsibility? He Yi: I think that whether it's Google or other platforms, when each platform does this, the first thing to consider is who my users are and what their use cases are. Therefore, each platform has different needs regarding the use of AI and AI Agents. From a purely AI perspective, firstly, we can use it for daily payments; secondly, we can use it for wealth management; and thirdly, we can use it for investment. However, this doesn't mean every user needs to constantly run trades with their Agent. I think the first step, and the most important for users, is understanding the most basic knowledge. Many users have no concept of investing. When the market goes up, they think it's CZ manipulating the market; when the market goes down, they think CZ is manipulating the market, as if there's a divine hand at work. This kind of thinking isn't a mature investment perspective. Therefore, I think AI on platforms like ours should help users make correct judgments and decisions. We started Binance Academy a long time ago, creating many tutorials, and also Binance Square. But Square is now more diverse, with all kinds of people. Some write macro articles, which may not get much traffic; others might dance in a live stream and get more traffic, but that's human nature. This doesn't mean what you're doing is meaningless. Those who want to see it will still see it, and those who don't will close it even if you put it in front of them. But at least as a platform, you should provide this knowledge to users, giving them some understanding of investing. If crypto itself is lowering the barrier to entry in finance—24-hour trading, transactions starting at just $5—allowing people in many countries around the world, even those not in the US, to easily access quality investment opportunities, then I think the greatest significance of AI is actually intelligent equality. Some people have asked me, when everyone is using AI, doesn't that bring us back to the same starting line? However, I believe that even if everyone has the same tools, like everyone having a phone, a computer, and internet access, there will always be a group of people who use that phone or computer to find their own path to success, leveling up and overcoming challenges. But some people, even if you give them a phone and a computer, will only use them for their own purposes. That's their choice, but the prerequisite is that you've given them the opportunity. If you create AI and put it in front of them, it's their problem if they don't use it; but if they don't, that's our problem. Question: Which positions at Binance have already substantially improved efficiency through AI? Has AI led to personnel adjustments? He Yi: Actually, I initially strongly advocated for the use of AI in customer service because Binance has a large user base, and we have a lot of customer service staff. There are also content moderation, KYB, and KYC, which involve a lot of personnel. AI efficiency has improved, but it's not as easy as people imagine. You can think of it as roughly three layers. The first layer is having a large amount of data, the middle layer is your own trained vertical models, and above that are large models, whether using OpenAI, DeepSeek, or other models. Even if you have a perfect, most expensive large model, it doesn't mean you can directly integrate it and solve the problem. You first need to clean your data. So we invested heavily in AI in the early stages and made many attempts, but ultimately found that our data wasn't clean enough or accurate enough. When ChatGPT first came out, I said it could definitely replace customer service, so we started having our team recruit people to build large models. We worked on it for a long time, a year, with very little success. Later, DeepSeek came out, along with open-source models. We retrained and cleaned the data, structuring all the data step by step, and only then did we start to see results. Our so-called efficiency improvement, I think, happened gradually. But I think a bigger reflection is that the requirements for talent will be different in the future. Previously, typical large companies were like assembly lines; although everyone was a developer and an engineer, they were actually working in an assembly-line manner. Especially some large Chinese companies, for management purposes, made the organization more structured. Western companies, on the other hand, might have more full-stack talent. You'll find that when this structured organization encounters AI, it might improve the quality of work in a certain link, but it doesn't change the original structured hierarchy. So you'll find that talent in the AI ​​era doesn't necessarily need a computer science background, nor does it necessarily have the kind of background we used to require. You might be able to handle many things using natural language. I myself am learning as I go. In this process, a major reflection I've had is that with the arrival of the AI ​​era, just like electricity has arrived, the skill of making candles in a candle factory may no longer be as crucial. We are currently reopening recruitment to bring in more fresh talent. I think the most important quality for AI talent in this new era is initiative—the ability to learn proactively. Initiative and learning ability may be more important than your academic qualifications or background. Overall, we've invested a lot, conducted many tests, and are constantly reflecting, but **we haven't actually significantly reduced our staff because of AI.** What I observed in the second half of the year was a change in our talent profile. In departments where AI applications are more mature, we didn't significantly increase hiring, but we also didn't significantly reduce staff. Overall, I think we're still feeling our way forward. When the AI ​​era arrives, could these types of jobs be merged, becoming new job requirements instead of being layered or structured assembly lines? I think our organizational structure may have reached a point where it needs to change. From Cryptocurrency Exchange to Global Financial Platform Question: Binance has been very active in the traditional financial sector this year, collaborating extensively with securities firms and launching numerous stock-related investment products. How is Binance's business progressing in this area? How do you view the impact of traditional financial assets on the crypto market? I think the essence isn't about Binance necessarily winning by offering stocks, but rather about your user profile and user demographics when developing a new product. For example, a couple of days ago, before US stocks even started trading, the price of Nvidia on the platform suddenly surged. So you can understand it as achieving price discovery earlier. Sometimes, weekend news also clearly reflects this in prices. Secondly, I don't think offering stocks is about directly competing with Robinhood. Robinhood primarily focuses on the US market, and we can't really target the US market. This means that, under this structure, our user profile and the needs of Americans are different. What we're addressing is lowering the barriers to trading, allowing users to buy and sell whenever they want. So what it actually solves is the problem of different user groups, different user needs, and price discovery. This includes some Pre-IPO Perps (pre-IPO perpetual contracts), which are also a path for the public to achieve price discovery. Some people might think that Binance is now involved in stocks, commodities, gold, silver, and oil, so what about Crypto? They might think, "There's no way to survive; all the money is going into stocks." But I don't agree. Since starting my exchange business in 2017, my view has been that a good token should be built on a good business model, with cash flow, revenue, and profit. Your business needs to be good to empower your token; only on this foundation can your cycle run. But this goes against human nature. Why does it go against human nature? Starting from scratch, some people become worth tens of millions, ready to sell their tokens immediately. This has been a recurring phenomenon in the cryptocurrency world over the past decade. You'll find many people with impressive backgrounds sell their tokens, retire, and move on to the AI ​​industry. If everyone says the industry is declining, who is responsible for this decline? Reflecting on this, I believe in the principle of "Do not do to others what you would not have them do to you." If I were an ordinary user, what would I want? I would want to be able to buy valuable assets in the world, not assets that rise today and fall to zero tomorrow. Therefore, based on this underlying logic, we began to bring various global assets to the platform. Essentially, Binance should be a platform where users are responsible for their own investment decisions, but they can find top global assets on the platform. Whether they want to go long or short, they can. If I really don't understand, or I'm a newbie, I can start by investing in stablecoins and learning. Based on this logic, this is why we made these changes and adjustments to our investment targets and categories. In terms of product offerings, in 2017 and 2018, we only offered spot trading. That was during a bear market; although we had become the world's largest exchange, the market was in turmoil because prices were falling every day. Personally, I didn't like futures contracts before because many users who lost money trading futures would seek redress and resort to insults. I felt this product was too risky, so I never invested. But that bear market taught me a valuable lesson; I eventually discovered that short selling still has its market. When the market is only going down, and everyone knows it's going down, there are at least trading opportunities. So essentially, this is a structural adjustment of investment categories and products. Once you've made this structural adjustment, you can step back and look at it from a more macro, longer-term perspective. Whether it's crypto products or the early days of internet IPOs, there were many bizarre companies with extremely high stock valuations that may have gone bankrupt or disappeared today. But in that era, before the dot-com bubble, they were all hot commodities. Looking further back at the development of the entire financial market, you'll also find that every market has a cycle. During economic upswings, various bubbles and booms make everyone feel like an investment genius, believing that everything they buy will rise in value. However, if we look at a longer timeframe, all the premiums brought about by these bubbles are problematic if you can't ultimately create a healthy business model that can scale, operate at low cost, and improve the lives of ordinary people. Even better, this includes lowering costs and increasing efficiency. Beyond these things, you should at least provide users with enjoyment, like in games. If you can't achieve this, then you're just creating a narrative, and no one should pay for that narrative. I think this industry has been focused on narratives for a long time. Even today, everyone is still chasing the question: why aren't there any new narratives emerging? However, the lack of new narratives doesn't mean Crypto hasn't penetrated into every household. Many countries in the world face inflation, and countless households are already using Crypto to solve cross-border money transfer problems. But these might not be very popular projects because they allow you to operate more efficiently and at a lower cost, making the world more stable. I know this viewpoint; I've been saying for years that you need a business model, and I've been ridiculed, told I don't understand. Since 2017, as someone working in the industry, I've probably heard people say: projects with business models and revenue aren't worth much. But I think, ultimately, we still need to return to common business sense. Question: A good financial market should possess liquidity, investment and financing, and price discovery functions. How will Binance address liquidity issues in the stock and stock tokenization sectors in the future? Will it introduce a mature market maker system? Regarding asset access, will it expand to Hong Kong stocks, Singapore markets, etc.? Furthermore, what further thoughts does Binance have on the price discovery function for pre-IPO products? He Yi: I'll start with liquidity. Because people generally understand Binance as just an exchange. This is perhaps a hurdle we need to overcome in our development; people's first reaction is still to see you as a cryptocurrency exchange. But in reality, Binance's business is now very diversified. As mentioned earlier, we already have over 8,000 stock instruments. Regarding the Crypto portion, we haven't personally participated in market making for many years, but we do offer rebates. If your trading volume is large, you can join the market maker program. When your trading volume meets the requirements and you provide good liquidity, you can receive different levels of rebates based on your ranking. This is our publicly available market maker program. With the expansion of the underlying assets, there are indeed two points. First, when we directly introduced these 8,000 stock assets, we didn't actually introduce the liquidity behind them. We didn't consider this issue when we did this before; we directly connected to the pool but didn't consider the liquidity problem. This is currently being revamped, and I understand that it should soon be able to directly connect to the liquidity of traditional brokerages. Therefore, the liquidity problem for the pure stock portion can be solved. The second part can be understood as us mapping stocks and tokens one-to-one. We ourselves do not participate in market making, and we operate under the supervision of ADGM, ensuring transparency in all operations. The second issue is asset issuance. We are currently discussing this with various exchanges. The most popular assets on each exchange are likely those representing the hottest themes at the moment. For example, stocks related to the AI ​​upstream and downstream ecosystem might be popular, while some traditional stocks might be ignored. Therefore, we don't put all global stocks on our platform; instead, we look for assets with high popularity and attention. For many large institutions, this could be a supplement to their traditional financial markets, or even a hedging tool for going long or short. We are currently discussing with various exchanges whether a stock can be tokenized from day one if tokenization is acceptable. If local exchanges cannot provide sufficient liquidity for certain assets, some startups may have a good foundation but face very high listing costs in the US or Hong Kong. There are actually many good companies worldwide with healthy profit models and potential. However, they may have considered IPOs in the past but abandoned them due to high costs. Could such companies choose smaller exchanges and directly pursue tokenization? I think the regulatory principles are sound, but ultimately, standard auditing procedures must be followed, such as IPO auditing and financial reporting. Compared to the past, when the cryptocurrency market had virtually no entry barriers, at least it has a regulated and standardized listing process. This is somewhat like going back from complete freedom and decentralization. But actually, it's all about trying to navigate between these two extremes. Over the past decade, we've seen many problems on the completely free and decentralized side; on the side of particularly strict regulation, some experimentation is also needed. Ultimately, it comes down to what kind of assets you can offer these users, rather than assets that go to zero after speculation. The third point is price discovery. I think price discovery is a dynamic process. Whether it's the cases I just mentioned or the pre-IPO cases, they all demonstrate that our user base is quite good. If you look at traditional financial markets, whether it's Hong Kong stocks or A-shares, Binance's scale is quite impressive in terms of trading volume. We may be a little smaller than US stocks or A-shares, and we can't directly say we're comparable to Hong Kong stocks, but in terms of global liquidity, our scale is quite similar. Question: Is it possible that TikTok or DeepSeek will be listed on Binance for pre-IPO trading in the future? He Yi: We should have already opened some A-share related contracts. However, I think listing is still heavily regulated, and it depends on the regulators. For example, our listing on the US stock market was done in cooperation with a licensed third party, and then with the approval of our regulatory agencies. If Chinese regulators say that Binance can sell A-shares here, we would certainly welcome that. This would help Chinese entrepreneurs better access global capital, lower the financing threshold, and allow people all over the world to buy Chinese stocks. This would be a positive signal for the entire Chinese financial market. But I think it still depends on the regulatory agencies' acceptance, the regulatory process, or where they deem the appropriate time to go. The Biggest Challenge in the Crypto Industry: Asset Hollowing Out Question: Binance's previous growth came more from retail users, but now it's gradually moving towards institutionalization. What are your views on Binance's current and next stage of development, and the future development of the entire crypto industry? He Yi: First of all, Binance's business has always been a crypto-native company. It's not that traditional finance looked down on us, but people in traditional finance generally disregarded cryptocurrencies in the early days. Today, whether it's BlackRock or other traditional financial institutions, they have become our partners. We feel this is a small step forward and something to be proud of. Essentially, it's because they saw the changes brought about by blockchain. So, this change actually happens gradually and subtly, rather than being a sudden, landmark event. In this process, we've seen many quantitative firms starting to use perpetual contracts (PERS) to hedge their existing stock holdings. This includes many ETF-making institutions; for example, some of the largest ETF companies in Asia have approached us asking if they can directly sell their ETFs to users on their platforms. If Binance is simply considered a brokerage firm, it's one of the top-ranked brokerages globally. In this process, some factors can slow it down, such as the regulatory understanding and caution regarding this matter. Of course, this also includes the inevitable impact of a new technology on traditional, established interest structures, which can also lead to backlash. So you'll find that the world moves forward in a process of constant adjustment, with each side pushing the other forward. I have great confidence in the entire technology industry, or rather, in the transformative impact of blockchain on traditional finance. It's not fundamentally a change on the asset side, but rather a change from the underlying structure and technology layer to operations, asset discovery, and price discovery. But this change isn't something that ends with a simple switch being flipped. It's more like electric lights replacing candles; first, some people turn on the lights, and then more people abandon candles. I believe the changes technology brings to humanity are a gradual, ongoing process. Speaking of the future, as mentioned earlier, are people worried that everyone in the crypto world will move into the AI ​​field? For example, electric vehicle technology, in my memory, is over a century old. But its actual application and widespread operation have only occurred in the last ten or twenty years. But is this technology meaningless? No, it's just temporarily shelved. There could be a thousand reasons for this shelving. The traditional automotive industry, whether in the US or some European countries, was a significant source of revenue, and the emergence of electric vehicles might pose a threat to it. However, every technology, as long as it brings progress and efficiency improvements to society, ultimately has its value. Today, people might think AI and Crypto are in competition, but I don't see it that way. If you understand it that way, AI is a threat to every industry. AI is a threat to graphic designers, writers, journalists, and investors, but it may pose the greatest threat to coders right now. Therefore, it is actually empowering your industry. Ultimately, it depends on what the industry produces and who truly utilizes it. Question: Recently, the crypto market has lacked high-quality new projects, and asset issuance activities such as IEOs have also decreased. Will this affect Binance's revenue? How does Binance view the current asset issuance market? He Yi: Every time a new asset is launched, everyone assumes it's a money-making opportunity. When we did IEOs in 2019, because of Binance's influence in the crypto industry, if you weren't listed on Binance, listing elsewhere wouldn't make much difference. So, if you listed on Binance, we'd offer a discount, and that discount would be distributed directly to everyone, allowing them to buy your assets at a discount. Essentially, it was a discounted initial offering, a way to give back to the community. I think this approach lasted for about two or three years, until finally, it became unsustainable. Why did it become unsustainable? Because previously, if the valuation was 100 million, a 50% or 30% discount was acceptable. But in the last cycle, the valuations of projects were already very high, so discounting didn't help. So you realize that the **IEO discount route** is no longer viable. You can only negotiate with project teams that are still willing to sell at a discount to users and are willing to use this funding channel to build their projects. But when others see that they can actually issue directly on a DEX without paying you fees, even though you're selling to users, why should they offer a discount? They can sell directly. In our second cycle, we actually did Alpha. Alpha is essentially based on the same logic. Spot trading has its standards, but Alpha itself is an on-chain transaction. If a project doesn't quite meet the spot trading standards, but you're willing to give money to people, you can also go through the Alpha route. Alpha distributed nearly $1 billion in benefits to its users; if not $1 billion, at least $800 million. The exact figure may have been calculated, as prices fluctuate with coin price changes. However, based on the initial pricing, it certainly provided significant benefits to many ordinary people. This distribution continued for about a year, but ultimately, it became difficult to continue. Why? Because the Alpha team stated, "We're not making money." Therefore, the fundamental issue wasn't the model, but rather the lack of good projects. Without good projects, forcing participation will inevitably lead to problems. Of course, some early adopters with good foresight at least had some opportunities to profit. As for the exchange, a few years ago, during an employee interview, I asked, "What do you think is most important for an exchange?" I think one of the most important things for exchanges is maintaining the balance of this ecosystem. Over the years, whether it's IEOs or Alpha, we've been trying to get projects that have raised significant funds to distribute money to retail investors. But then one day, the project team tells you, "I'm out of money, there's no use in contacting me." What happens then? So I think the biggest problem in the entire industry right now is asset hollowing out—the lack of good assets. Because if there aren't good assets, what's the difference between listing and not listing? You just asked if the absence of IEOs will affect Binance's revenue? If you ask me, I definitely hope the market rises every day, because for me, a bull market is definitely the time to really make money. Users have a particularly strong willingness to trade, and our main business model is to earn transaction fees. All these IEO activities, frankly speaking, are benefits for users and also help maintain the ecological balance of the entire market. This is because the capabilities of different participants in the market are completely asymmetrical. Quantitative institutions have the best models, macro research, and have done a lot of research on the market. But later you find that project teams in the market say they have no money, and institutions may stop trading. Although they made some money before, now many transactions have stopped. Therefore, as an exchange, you must constantly maintain the balance of the ecosystem. You must continuously ensure that users can use your platform, not just for trading, but because the platform is useful to them. They can invest their spare money, and even if they don't have spare money, they can still use it every day. This is our logic. Retail investors say, "Now that Alpha has stopped, you're not providing any financial support anymore." Think about where the term "financial support" comes from. It's because I'm here to profit; if I can profit, it's considered financial support. If I lose even a dollar, it's no longer financial support. So ultimately, you realize you're constantly trying to balance this ecosystem. Of course, you'll eventually find that the most important thing for balancing this ecosystem is actually good assets. That's why we've started thinking again: when the entire market is falling, where are the good assets and good products? Question: Faced with the current pessimistic market sentiment, how do you view market cycles and future investment opportunities? He Yi: I still have confidence in the market. I strongly believe in two things: cycles and value investing. In a long-term cycle, good assets, even those with poor liquidity, are still good assets. However, for me, liquidity is more important because it's determined by my profession. For example, properties in Lujiazui, Shanghai; Shenzhen Bay; and Manhattan—these assets have value, but their liquidity might not be that good. Therefore, my profession dictates that I consider liquidity the primary factor. Only when there is liquidity do I consider what the best assets are. Essentially, most people understand the meaning of cycles: there will always be ups and downs, always people predicting a downturn and always people predicting a upturn. Everyone understands what valuable assets are, but the difficulty lies in "knowing is easy, doing is hard." You understand this, but can you really do it? Look at Nvidia, it just went up, then it went down again. Many people think, "Forget it, I'll sell." Most people have this mentality: knowing is easy, doing is hard. So it's not that the market doesn't have money, it's that people are afraid to spend it. Moreover, we're currently in a global economic downturn, so this so-called pessimism will occur in every market. Question: Recently, the pace of Binance Alpha's activities has changed. What changes will there be in Alpha's positioning and pace in the future? How do you view the related rumors in the market? He Yi: First, our original intention was to give benefits to users, but we didn't intend to only give benefits to studios.

    If you offer benefits, there will definitely be people who come specifically for those benefits. Sometimes, retail investors aren't as keen on spotting these money-making opportunities. But essentially, what Binance wants to do is simply offer some benefits to Real Users—it's that simple.

    This is about Alpha's positioning itself.

    Above this positioning, are Alpha users Binance's core source of revenue? Of course not.

    Therefore, I don't necessarily need to specifically issue assets for Alpha. I can only say that, given good underlying assets, if I can provide benefits to users, I will do my best to perfect the process of offering benefits to users.

    Essentially, as long as there are good underlying assets in the market, the market may heat up or cool down.

    However, as long as the platform itself remains neutral and maintains the balance of the ecosystem as much as possible, and even if users don't trade, they can still use these products on the platform for daily financial management or payments. This is something we've been thinking about for a long time. Global Compliance, Organizational Capabilities, and Binance's Next Decade Question: What are Binance's key development priorities and expectations in the Asian market? Furthermore, Binance used to be a highly distributed organization, but now it has more regulated entities. What new challenges does this change pose to Binance's organizational capabilities? He Yi: First, if you look at demographics, Asia's population exceeds 50% of the world's total. I don't remember the exact number, but Asia accounts for a large portion of the world's population. This directly determines that if you want to achieve mass appeal, Asia is a very important market. Based on this, is there a tiered system? Yes. Countries with large populations are definitely a high priority, as are economically developed countries. Under this framework, we are indeed communicating simultaneously with regulatory agencies in hundreds of countries. Progress may vary in different countries. For example, in some countries, we may have already entered their regulatory sandbox. However, different countries have different regulatory bodies; some are central banks, some are the SEC (formerly responsible for stocks) which also oversees crypto, some are independent regulatory bodies, and some countries previously lacked a crypto-related regulatory framework. You might have a license but not be listed on the App Store; or you might be listed on the App Store, but the tax policy in that country is not yet clear. Local regulatory agencies might say, "Go ahead and do it; we'll discuss tax issues later." Various scenarios exist. You'll find that every country and every regulatory agency has completely different priorities. For example, some countries are very concerned about taxes, some are very concerned about inflation, and in some countries, one regulatory department might approve your application, but another might not allow you to proceed to the next step. Some countries might even approve it in principle, but in principle, they don't allow foreign ownership to exceed 50% or 40%. But I believe there are always more solutions than problems. Essentially, in any industry, the growth curve is relatively steep at the beginning. However, when you truly aim for mass adoption, you face various regulatory issues and compliance costs, which is normal. We cannot regard this rapid, exponential growth as the norm. Any company will likely experience exponential growth, then enter a relatively stable phase, before seeking new growth opportunities. Regarding the challenges to the organization itself, I feel that organizational capabilities have actually improved significantly over the past few years; I've personally witnessed this. The organization's capabilities are constantly evolving. My requirement for organizational capability iteration is that it should be able to function well on its own even without my intervention. Therefore, we have recruited some very high-quality talent in the past few years. They may have worked in regulatory systems or similar companies, and much of their experience can be reused. So I think our team's overall organizational capabilities have improved. Foresight News: Shortly after Binance was founded in 2017, it reached the position of the world's number one cryptocurrency exchange. For a long time afterward, Binance maintained its number one position. If we extend our timeframe to the next ten years, from 2027 to 2037, what do you think is most likely to defeat Binance? Is it AI, regulation, hackers, or something new that hasn't yet emerged? Just like today, AI is the challenge to search engines, something that probably no one expected ten years ago. He Yi: I think it's something new that hasn't yet emerged. Foresight News: Could you elaborate? As CEO, what are you most anxious about right now? Or, what do you think poses the greatest threat to Binance? He Yi: I think the biggest threat always comes from within. "Internal" means that people are afraid of being subjective, afraid of not knowing. People usually think they know, but in reality, many don't. So, I think there are two key words within Binance over the past two years, which may have been rarely mentioned before, but are mentioned more often now. The first is "objectivity," which means being truthful and pragmatic. Being truthful means asking yourself, what is your actual position in the market? You might be the largest globally, but in some niche markets, like Thailand, we're not the largest. Because local competitors are locals, speak the local language, offer local services, and their products are very localized, like your next-door neighbor. So essentially, I think iterative development of capabilities is very important, but it must be based on seeking truth and being pragmatic. The second key word, I think, is "fairness." I may not need a platform that guarantees I can make money, but I need a fair and reasonable platform. As an employee, I may not be able to find a perfect boss, but I hope my boss is fair. Therefore, I think organizational failures often stem from within, not from without. Whether it's innovation or talent, when your team stops growing, you stop growing. Foresight News: What are some obvious signs that a team has stopped growing? For example, when the number of employees reaches a certain size? He Yi: I don't think it has anything to do with the number of people. It probably includes several things: Do you still have curiosity? Are you still actively learning? Do you have ownership? Or, as you often hear in large companies, "That's not my scope of responsibility." These are probably what I'm more concerned about.

data.title: US household stock exposure hits record high; frenzied buying continues despite AI crash.
data.description:
Author: Bu Shuqing, Wall Street Insights

Americans are betting more and more of their wealth on the stock market! Stocks now account for over 40% of American household financial assets, a new high since the 1950s. This year, over $450 billion has flowed into US stock funds, and even with the plunge in AI concept stocks and the sharp fluctuations in the US stock market, bargain hunters continue to pour in. When household wealth is so deeply intertwined with the stock market, a reversal of this multi-year bull market could have an impact that extends beyond Wall Street, directly affecting American households.

American households' bets on the stock market have reached an all-time high, and even with the recent sharp decline in AI stocks, retail investor funds continue to pour in. This four-year bull market is pushing millions of ordinary investors into unprecedented risk exposure, and the trajectory of their wealth will largely determine whether the market can stabilize.

According to Deutsche Bank's analysis of EPFR data, new inflows into ETFs and mutual funds tracking US stocks this year have exceeded $450 billion, potentially setting a new record. Even amidst the complete collapse of AI trading and severe market volatility in the past month, US equity funds still saw net inflows of over $141 billion in November alone—a period during which the S&P 500 had already fallen 3.4%. Data from Ed Clissold, chief US strategist at Ned Davis Research, shows that US stocks now account for over 40% of total US household financial assets, a record high since records began in the 1950s. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 has fallen 6.7% from its October high, and the Nasdaq Composite has retreated 13% from its record high in early October, remaining in a technical correction phase. Economists at Capital Economics warn that if the sell-off continues, it could quickly drag down consumer spending.

Funds continue to pour in, setting a new record for the longest consecutive net inflow

The enthusiasm of retail investors is particularly evident in the data. EPFR data shows that as of September this year, US equity funds have seen net inflows for 13 consecutive months, the longest consecutive net inflow record since the database began recording in 2000.

Deutsche Bank equity strategist Parag Thatte said: "This sell-off has been met with a massive inflow of funds into US equity funds."

These inflows include both passive funds automatically invested through retirement accounts such as 401(k) and active "buy on dips" operations by investors. Data from State Street Investment Management shows that ETFs have attracted more than $880 billion in new funds this year, also setting a record; in contrast, mutual funds have recorded net outflows.

Universal Market Entry: AI Trading Becomes a Core Variable in Wealth

Behind this round of capital inflows lies the wealth effect and investment inertia accumulated over the past three years by the excess returns driven by AI stocks. AI stocks have consistently propelled the market upward over the past three years, prompting many ordinary investors to increase their holdings.

Some Gen Z Americans have even abandoned their home purchase plans, redirecting funds originally intended for down payments to the stock market; Baby Boomers, who have long been advised to reduce their stock holdings, now hold a higher proportion of their portfolios; and many investors have borrowed funds this year to amplify their stock exposure.

Data from the New York Federal Reserve shows that in the mid-1980s, during Reagan's administration, less than 30% of households owned stocks; by the early 21st century, this proportion had exceeded 50%. The latest data from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances shows that approximately 56% of households currently own stocks.

AI Stock Plunge Tests Retail Investor Confidence; Market Stabilization Depends on Retail Funds. This round of AI-driven market volatility has lasted for weeks, affecting everything from the US midterm elections to the dramatic turmoil within Nvidia, making it difficult even for experienced investors to cope. US stocks recently recorded one of their worst weekly performances since the March 2020 pandemic collapse, with many AI-related stocks falling more than 40% from their highs, and the S&P 500 nearly erasing all of its year-to-date gains. JPMorgan Chase's Nikolaos Panigirtzoglou wrote in a report to clients earlier this month: "After the brutal deleveraging experienced by hedge funds in October, retail investor support is crucial for stabilizing AI trading in November." Goldman Sachs data shows that American households are the largest holders of US stocks. In the coming weeks, retail investors' confidence in a market rebound may be the key force preventing a further sharp decline. Wealth is deeply intertwined with the stock market, and consumer risks cannot be ignored. As the correlation between US household finances and the stock market becomes increasingly close, a continued sell-off will have far-reaching consequences beyond paper losses. Capital Economics economists recently pointed out that between February and April 2025, the decline in the S&P 500 quickly translated into a drop in consumer spending, at a time when Trump's escalating trade war triggered market concerns about an economic recession. Ed Yardeni, founder of Yardeni Research, describes this correlation as a "feedback loop"—a stock market decline suppresses consumption, which in turn impacts corporate profit expectations, further exacerbating market pressure. Thatte of Deutsche Bank also points out that sustained capital inflows are highly correlated with strong corporate profits. "If investors begin to doubt the ability of U.S. companies to continue generating profits, they may stop buying." For U.S. retail investors who are still buying on dips, this may be the most severe test since the start of the four-year bull market.

data.title: The Real Impact of AI on the Economy and Advice for Young People
data.description:
Author: Mu Feng; Source: The Sun Also Rises

Yesterday, Feng Ji, the creator of *Black Myth: Wukong*, published an article titled "The Most Important Issue in the Post-AI Era," proposing that "while adhering to the principle of distribution according to work, the excess material wealth created by AI replacing human labor in the future should be equally distributed to everyone." The article is quite readable.

Within less than a year, many industries that once relied on human intelligence have been impacted by AI, and traditional jobs have been widely affected. What is the essence of the AI ​​substitution effect, and what is the substance of its impact on the economy? These questions are not only major research topics but also very real issues.

The author argues that, currently, the job substitution effect of AI, from an economic perspective, manifests as a shift from "human-to-human exchange" to "human-to-AI exchange." Human economies arise from mutual demand and scarcity of supply; exchange fulfills these needs, leading to social division of labor and ultimately increased efficiency. From individuals to regions to nations, exchange is a prerequisite for economic operation. As AI gradually replaces human intellectual labor in terms of content, progressing from simple to complex intellectual labor, the entire business model based on the exchange of human intellectual resources is the first to be impacted. What used to require programmers, AI does; what used to require human translators, AI does; what used to require artists, AI does; what used to require analysts, AI does… AI not only does it faster, but it does it better, and crucially, it's much cheaper than human labor. The exchange that once existed between humans and AI will disappear, replaced by an exchange with AI. This disappearing part is often the most traditional intellectual economy, that is, the so-called "specialized slots" that gradually formed after the rise of the industrial age—specific divisions of labor based on specialized learning and employment. The reason for this division of labor is that there was once exchange. Now everyone is exchanging with AI, so this part of the division of labor is unnecessary. Without the necessity of exchange, jobs will naturally disappear. However, two parts cannot disappear: first, the part that ultimately needs to be determined or decided by humans, that is, humans as the final gatekeepers and decision-makers; second, the part that generates demand, because only humans have genuine demand, AI itself has no demand, only AI companies have the demand to charge. Therefore, essentially, the impact of AI on the economy is a supply-side shock. Services that were once provided by many industries and millions of people through the division of labor in society are now being undertaken by AI alone. This supply substitution leads to the disappearance of exchange, and consequently, employment problems. This is the greatest challenge ever encountered in the history of human economics. Because past technological revolutions have always started with the replacement of certain industries, gradually replacing them, giving other industries ample time to adjust. Simultaneously, educational adjustments further strengthen the division of labor, allowing the entire economic structure to achieve a new balance. Why, then, do some still argue that relying on traditional "education and training" is beneficial for adapting to the new environment in the face of AI's impact? Because this is a method used in past technological revolutions, effective then, but largely meaningless in the AI ​​era. AI itself is constantly eliminating professional skills, while education and training aim to create and enter those skills—a mindset from the industrial age. The author believes that a deep understanding of how AI will shape the future human economy and even society requires a cautious and rigorous forward-looking perspective. Realistically speaking, positions ultimately determined or decided by humans are always scarce; they are either management positions or professional positions requiring considerable seniority. Therefore, for individuals, the most important thing in the AI ​​era is to deeply understand human needs, have a concrete perception of human life, and become individuals capable of discovering and creating needs to the fullest extent in an era of abundant human intelligence. Thus, looking at the end from the beginning, the traditional education system, which began in the industrial age and aimed at entering a specific professional field, is completely outdated. This doesn't mean all professional specializations have become ineffective, but rather that the era of hoping to enter through a few certificates and then rise rapidly through the ranks is over. Don't believe it? Ask those gifted students; how much do their entry into cutting-edge companies and their receipt of top-paying offers have to do with formal schooling and professional certificates? Currently, school education, in terms of employment selection, still offers a relatively positive contribution by essentially screening based on intelligence. However, this process is too costly and exhausting, wasting the talents of many students. Feng Ji lamented that he "intensively tested a batch of web games created with the newly released Fable 5.2, and many of them were surprisingly well-made; a few even made me lose track of time while playing." It's worth noting that previously, entering the game industry and joining a major company required studying at least a top-tier university (985 or higher) in a very specific major, and then undergoing fierce selection to even get started. The frequently recommended game "Holding Weapons in Song" was created by several ordinary individuals—ride-hailing drivers, delivery workers, stay-at-home mothers, and so on. Without diligent study at prestigious film schools like the Beijing Film Academy and the Central Academy of Drama, without joining mainstream film and television companies, and without sufficient film and television capital support, would it have been possible to achieve this level of viewership? Feng Ji's observations and insights are accurate. The essence of the AI ​​era is a massive explosion in the supply side of intellectual resources. Everything previously limited by specialized fields will be broken through by the development of AI. This also means that the "professional monopoly supply" previously formed by specialized fields will be dismantled one by one. Those who previously said "you don't understand" the demand side will face elimination, because AI not only understands but can also respond to needs more effectively. The AI ​​era is an era where demand reigns supreme. Without understanding and creating demand, an abundance of supply is meaningless. The author's ultimate point is that our current education system is completely outdated. This isn't anyone's fault, as humanity has never been prepared for this, globally. Not only that, but every industry was unprepared, let alone education. However, in East Asia, where grades and exams are extremely important, parents and students must prioritize their future, especially given the current lack of a suitable direction in the broader educational environment. Frankly, even five years from now, let alone ten, the economic landscape and employment changes are difficult to predict. Could you have imagined AI short dramas developing to their current state a year ago? As individuals, we need to be "involved" and experience it firsthand. We shouldn't shield students from AI simply because it brings entertainment. "No pain, no gain"—this was the motto of an era of extreme material scarcity. Knowing only how to endure hardship, without deeply understanding the real needs of millions of consumers, meant only continued suffering in the future. Because if you lack even the imagination to "aspire to a better life," who will consume for you? In an era of abundant productivity and intellectual resources, creators own the future. We cannot raise young people in the AI ​​era according to the standards of the industrial age. They need opportunities to engage with reality, to realize the rapid changes brought about by AI, to understand the enormous transformation taking place in human society, and to feel that excitement. Many schools are changing now, but some parents haven't. The author understands that Feng Ji and many others hold similar views, namely that the enormous wealth of the AI ​​industry should be shared by all people in the AI ​​era. Frankly speaking, the human world still lacks such an economic tool. For example, the "universal income plan" repeatedly mentioned in Europe and America—how to achieve it is a critical question. As AI users, we believe that AI companies are earning income from the replaced humans, but in reality, AI token fees are extremely low. Even leading large-scale models charge much less than human labor, while being far more efficient and of higher quality. In other words, because exchange is disappearing, rather than simply replacing it, the total economic output of industries affected by AI is continuously declining. But is the new economic output arising from AI continuously rising and making up for the previous decline? We haven't seen this happen yet; there's no empirical data, and individuals don't feel it either. Furthermore, from the perspective of AI companies, it's still the beginning of a period of heavy asset investment. All previously asset-light internet companies, upon entering the AI ​​competition, have invariably faced heavy asset pressure; large-scale computing power purchases are essentially buying a ticket to the future. Therefore, currently, we are still in the takeoff stage for AI. The overall economic balance has not yet been established. If AI can satisfy the intellectual activities previously requiring high-cost manual labor with low pricing for a long time, then there will be no extra "revenue" to distribute to the public. Even large-scale taxation of AI companies would not be sufficient. At this point, we realize that the economic, fiscal, and debt systems established since the Industrial Revolution are completely incompatible with the AI ​​era of abundant material and intellectual resources. In other words, the entire economic structure faces restructuring. This level of restructuring is unprecedented since the Industrial Revolution. Of course, it's important to understand that abundant productivity and intellectual resources are undoubtedly most beneficial to humanity, because paper wealth is illusory, while material wealth is real. Under this premise, how to adjust the distribution structure is a huge challenge that the entire world will face in the future, not just a problem for one country. Don't assume that working for a large company means you can relax and do nothing for life; that's not possible in the future. State-owned enterprises will lay off employees, and large factories can go bankrupt, but new companies will constantly emerge, and new forms of business will continue to appear. The author has previously analyzed the history of the USA Fortune 500, noting that most of the largest companies in the US at one time have disappeared over time. Many large companies will face significant adjustments in the AI ​​era. For ordinary people, the author's advice remains the same: have your own hobbies and interests, and develop them into productive activities, rather than just for consumption. Because future exchanges will be exchanges that can be completed between ordinary people. You can make your own games, compose your own songs, produce your own films and TV series, become an expert in a specific field, create a history video course loved by 500,000 people, or even create a paper-cutting art self-media platform, or even if you just love cooking. As long as you have enough interest and the willingness to get to the bottom of things, you can definitely have at least hundreds of thousands of followers, and you will never have to go hungry or cold again. This is the foundation for the survival of ordinary people in the future. The domestic market of 1.4 billion people is your biggest source of confidence, and of course, there are billions of dollars worth of overseas markets waiting for you to explore. Who says only large companies can go global? This is not to say that everyone has to become a self-employed individual in the AI ​​era, but rather that only by having sufficient sensitivity to demand, sufficient judgment of the market, and a deep understanding of industry development trends can an individual, even if they choose to work for a company in the future, have better judgment and development potential. These are also the basic requirements that companies will have for employees in the AI ​​era. If you are still young, you will definitely have a lot of negative voices around you, constantly telling you that everything the author is talking about can only be achieved by a few people, and most people simply cannot do it. When the author was young, he was surrounded by these voices as well. The only thing that can be confirmed is that those who do not try and make mistakes when they are young will only have regrets and negative emotions when they are older. Every attempt is a process of trial and error, but there's no right or wrong in it. The process of trying is more important than the result, because every effort you make will bring you huge gains. Regardless of whether you adjust your direction later, the gains in this process will have immense significance for your future life. Life is a process; experience is more important than the result. The cost of trial and error in the future will be hundreds or thousands of times lower than before. It's simply a matter of buying some tokens or starting a social media account. You won't have to travel to a place where you don't even speak the language like your ancestors did, nor will you have to use your savings of over a decade to open a store and hand over all the income to the landlord like your parents did. Why do so many people support open-source models and AI companies that keep token prices as low as possible? Because almost all large corporations in human history have ultimately ended up collecting rent. But only by minimizing the rent for the productivity that humanity depends on can we talk about the "complete liberation of humanity." Why did children from average-income families not have as many opportunities in the past? Because production tools cost money, and rent costs money, which ordinary families couldn't afford. It wasn't that they weren't willing to pursue their passions, but rather that their families couldn't support them. Therefore, they had to work to support themselves first. And most people, in this process, had already worn down their ideals. This is the biggest difference between the AI ​​era and the past. If we continue to support open-source models and keep token prices low, then most differences due to family background will be largely eliminated. Those exceptionally talented children from ordinary families will have more opportunities to try and fail, just like those from well-off families. This is greater equality of opportunity, and the meaning of progress.
