data.title: The threat of AI is escalating: Massive network outages sweep across the West.
data.description:
Author: Bao Yilong, Wall Street Insights

The British government was forced to shut down most of its social welfare system on Friday, following a week of cyber intrusions and service disruptions involving the US Treasury, CIA, and FIFA. Faced with this challenge, cybersecurity defense has spawned a huge commercial opportunity. An OpenAI executive stated that cybersecurity has become a core business with even greater potential than AI programming, with a market size far exceeding $300 billion, and is becoming a new engine reshaping the business landscape of tech giants.

A series of high-profile cyber incidents and system outages are intensely impacting core public sectors and commercial institutions in Europe and the US, exposing the severe vulnerabilities of outdated digital infrastructure in the age of artificial intelligence, and directly spurring fierce competition among AI giants for the commercialization of cybersecurity.

On November 27, according to the Financial Times, the British government was forced to shut down most of its social welfare system on Friday, becoming the latest security vulnerability exposed in critical infrastructure spanning the US and Europe. In the week prior, the US Treasury Department, the CIA, and FIFA were among the organizations embroiled in cyber intrusions and service disruptions. This wave of shutdowns and data breaches has sparked widespread concern across the transatlantic about escalating hacking attacks and has quickly become a commercial opportunity for tech giants. According to The Information, Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, recently stated that cybersecurity has the potential to become a more commercially viable business segment than AI programming. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar pointed out that external estimates of the global cybersecurity market size exceeding $300 billion still significantly underestimate the long-term growth potential of this field. Scott Wu, CEO of the US AI programming startup Cognition, warned on the podcast "Invest Like the Best" that, based on current trends, a large number of major data breaches are "almost inevitable" globally in the next 6 to 12 months, with Fortune 500 and Fortune 100 companies and government agencies all at high risk. As AI models become far more efficient than humans in vulnerability discovery and automated penetration testing, businesses and government agencies face higher compliance and defense expenditures to maintain business continuity. Model developers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are accelerating the establishment of security defense as a new core growth engine, attempting to reshape the commercial landscape in the multi-billion dollar cybersecurity market. Core institutions in Europe and the US have been attacked one after another, putting pressure on aging infrastructure. Since November, a series of high-profile cyber incidents and system outages have occurred, directly impacting public services, financial regulation, and business operations. According to the Financial Times, the UK Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), which manages the £330 billion UK welfare system, did not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack while urgently restoring online services on Friday. Just days earlier, the US Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) stated that it had taken some services offline due to a potential cyberattack that resulted in "unauthorized access" to its systems. Besides core government departments, international organizations and intelligence agencies have also been affected. This week, hackers breached FIFA's systems, stealing "personal and business information." According to The New York Times, the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence also recently discovered a cybersecurity vulnerability, leading to the leakage of some non-classified information. In the business sector, multiple data breaches since November have directly resulted in the grounding of some airlines and the disruption of digital banking platform services. However, not all system outages were directly caused by external hackers. Microsoft and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) also experienced network outages this month, resulting in blocked email access and the grounding of thousands of flights, respectively. According to the Financial Times, these outages actually stemmed from emergency updates performed by the relevant agencies to patch software vulnerabilities. Analysis indicates that the fundamental reason for the urgency of these agencies in upgrading their systems is the concern that cybercriminals and nation-state hacking groups are using AI tools to enhance their offensive capabilities. Attack patterns are crossing a critical point, shifting from "monopoles" to "swarms." The evolution of AI technology is fundamentally changing the speed, scale, and technical barriers of cyberattacks, prompting the industry to issue stern warnings about the security situation in the coming year. Rafe Pilling, Senior Director at cybersecurity company Sophos, stated that the recent series of incidents has inevitably raised concerns about their causes and the resilience of systems on which we rely daily. "The cyber threat landscape is not only becoming more complex, but also faster, easier to implement, and more crowded," he added, noting that the digital infrastructure upon which the world relies will face greater pressure in the coming year. In terms of attack patterns, the collaborative nature of AI agents is bringing a new industry turning point. Scott Wu, CEO of Cognition, attributes the surge in risk to the evolution of AI attack patterns from "monopoles" to "swarms." In the past, when a single AI agent performed a task, attackers were limited by time, energy, and technical capabilities, making it difficult to exhaust all attack paths. Now, a "swarm" of multiple AI agents operating collaboratively can attempt a massive number of attack paths in parallel, significantly increasing attack speed and coverage. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a bipartisan think tank, recently pointed out that the US Congress in 2027 will likely need to focus on addressing dangerous data breaches, which have recently severely impacted the normal operation of the US administration.

data.title: Apple and OpenAI have completely fallen out.
data.description:
Author: Little Bear Biscuit, BitpushNews

Two years ago, Apple brought ChatGPT into its iPhone; two years later, the two companies have taken each other to court.

Even more dramatically, the core designer who helped Apple create the iPhone is now helping OpenAI explore the next generation of smart hardware, and the two sides are even accusing each other of stealing trade secrets.

According to the Financial Times, on November 27th local time, OpenAI officially filed a countersuit against Apple. A business dispute that has lasted for months is evolving into a head-on confrontation between two of Silicon Valley's tech giants.

A Business Marriage with Hidden Motives

In the summer of 2024, generative AI swept through Silicon Valley. Microsoft seized the initiative through its collaboration with OpenAI, Google accelerated its deployment of Gemini, while Apple, which has always been adept at defining technological trends, appeared somewhat passive.

At that year's Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC), Apple officially launched Apple Intelligence and announced the integration of ChatGPT into Siri and the system's writing tools.

At that year's Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC), Apple officially launched Apple Intelligence and announced the integration of ChatGPT into Siri and the system's writing tools.

This seemed like a near-perfect business alliance at the time. Apple had a massive global user base for hardware but desperately needed leading AI technology; OpenAI possessed highly sought-after large-scale models but lacked its own hardware and operating system. One had an entry point, the other had the technology; both sides got what they needed. However, this relationship was fraught with problems from the start: Apple wanted AI to be a feature within its ecosystem, while OpenAI likely aimed to create a new platform independent of the existing ecosystem. The two companies' ultimate goals were not aligned. $6.4 Billion: OpenAI Enters Apple's Core Market The real turning point came in May 2025. OpenAI announced its acquisition of AI hardware startup io for approximately $6.4 billion. The key figure behind this company was none other than Apple's former Chief Design Officer, Jony Ive. From the iMac and iPod to the iPhone, Ive was involved in creating Apple's most iconic products and was one of the most important figures at Apple during the Jobs era. Now, this design master who once helped Apple change the world has begun collaborating with Alter to explore next-generation AI hardware. OpenAI's ambitions are not hard to see: it is no longer content with simply creating software that runs on other people's devices, but hopes to have its own hardware entry point. This means that partners who originally provided AI capabilities to Apple are now expanding their business into Apple's territory. More subtly, OpenAI has not only taken away Apple's former design spirit, but has also attracted a large number of Apple employees with experience in consumer electronics R&D. Partners are becoming potential competitors. Former allies have long since drifted apart. In fact, the deterioration of their relationship was foreshadowed. In May 2026, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was dissatisfied with the actual commercial benefits of its partnership with Apple and began exploring the possibility of legal action. The core issue is that while ChatGPT has entered Apple's ecosystem, the user entry point remains in Apple's hands. When and how users access ChatGPT largely depends on Apple's system design. This is also a classic business contradiction in the tech industry: who truly owns the users—the platform or the service provider? Apple certainly doesn't want Siri to become a springboard for ChatGPT, and OpenAI doesn't want to remain a behind-the-scenes player in the Apple ecosystem forever. For OpenAI, having its own hardware not only means opening up new revenue streams but also the opportunity to break free from dependence on other tech giants' platforms. From talent poaching to mutual lawsuits, relations have finally broken down. In July of this year, Apple took the initiative, suing OpenAI and two former Apple employees. Apple accused them of improperly obtaining company secrets to assist OpenAI in developing consumer AI hardware. One of the defendants, Tang Tan, was Apple's Vice President of Product Design. OpenAI denies the allegations. On November 27th, OpenAI officially launched its counterattack. According to Reuters, OpenAI's countersuit mainly involves three aspects: Trade secrets: Apple rehired a former OpenAI employee who had worked there for six months, a move OpenAI suspects involves confidential information about unreleased devices and future hardware plans. Supply chain: OpenAI accuses Apple of hindering hardware suppliers from collaborating with it. Talent mobility: OpenAI questions Apple's management of the personal devices and accounts of former employees, believing it is intended to restrict talent from flowing to competitors. OpenAI also stated in the lawsuit that approximately 400 Apple employees have jumped ship to Apple. Apple responded that OpenAI's countersuit is an attempt to divert attention from its original lawsuit. Of course, the trade secret allegations raised by both parties still await court proceedings and cannot be directly considered as proven facts. However, from talent and technology to the supply chain, the two sides are vying for almost all the core resources needed to create a consumer electronics product. What is Apple afraid of? What Apple really needs to be wary of is perhaps not OpenAI making another phone, but rather OpenAI creating a product that makes people less dependent on their phones. For the past decade or so, the basic business logic of the mobile internet has been: hardware carries the operating system, the operating system carries apps, and apps connect users and services. Apple happens to control a highly valuable link in this industry chain. But generative AI is challenging this interaction method. In the future, when you need to book a flight, reply to emails, buy goods, or handle work, you may no longer need to open five or six different apps; you might only need to issue a single command to AI. If AI becomes the primary entry point for human interaction with the digital world, then the commercial value of traditional operating systems, app stores, and even smartphones themselves may be redefined. This is the most noteworthy aspect of OpenAI's foray into the hardware field. Of course, creating an excellent AI application and building a successful consumer electronics product are two completely different things. Supply chain, mass production, battery life, cost, and user experience are all hurdles that OpenAI must overcome. Apple is not sitting idly by either. It possesses a mature hardware system, a massive user base, and strong ecosystem barriers; these advantages will not disappear overnight due to the emergence of AI. But the cruelest thing about the tech industry is that what truly disrupts you is often not your competitors, but players from another sector. In 2007, Steve Jobs redefined the mobile phone with the iPhone, and also changed the entire mobile internet. Nearly twenty years later, the design master who helped create the iPhone is joining forces with an AI company to try to explore a new world after smartphones. Will history rhyme again? It's too early to say. As AI giants start making hardware, and hardware giants accelerate their AI deployments, the original business boundaries of the tech industry are disappearing. The clash between Apple and OpenAI is a microcosm of the reshaping of the industry landscape in the AI ​​era.

data.title: The most important issue in the post-AI era
data.description:
Author: Feng Ji; Source: Feng Ji Yocar

When artificial intelligence (AI) massively replaces human labor in production, how should society view the value of human beings?

This question sounds like a philosophical discussion confined to an academic study, but if we extrapolate it from reality, it will soon collide with the livelihoods of countless households and the pressing choices they face, ultimately becoming a crucial political and economic question that determines how wealth and dignity are distributed.

If we define the "post-AI era" as an era in which AI has surpassed the intelligence of most humans in the vast majority of fields—I believe this is the most important question of the post-AI era, without exception.

If we define the "post-AI era" as an era in which AI has surpassed the intelligence of most humans in the vast majority of fields—I believe this is the most important question of the post-AI era, without exception.

Last weekend, my screen was almost split in two by two completely unrelated pieces of news. One half was in my old profession: GTA 6 rewrote the revenue record in the history of human entertainment, raising the commercial ceiling of the traditional content industry by a significant margin. The other half was in the AI ​​field: On Friday, news suddenly broke that the Riemann Hypothesis had been proven by AI. By Sunday, rumors began to circulate that cutting-edge models had made breakthroughs in the P vs NP problem. In the same week, I played a batch of newly released web games made with Fable 5.2. Many of them were surprisingly well-made, and I even lost track of time playing a few of them.

There is a public repository on GitHub that specifically summarizes the generated content of Fable 5.2

Source: https://github.com/fengyiqicoder/awesome-fable-5.2

Logically speaking, all of the above should be celebrated: the most massive IP masterpiece is refreshing the commercial ceiling, the oldest mathematical holy grail is loosening, and the most advanced creative tools are drastically dismantling professional barriers.

No matter how you look at it, this is a golden moment of human technological explosion.

But as I slumped in my chair, experiencing my usual dizziness and slump, another question swirled in my mind—"If AI solves math problems, AI makes games, what will happen to people if one day no one needs them anymore?" This question has been bothering me for years, and I've jotted down fragmented thoughts here and there. Until recently, these seemingly unrelated major events collided head-on, and I suddenly felt that the scattered threads of the past could finally be connected. After finishing writing, I realized it was a bit long and not convenient to fit into other platforms' news feeds, so I simply created this public account. If I have any more thoughts like these that I can't finish explaining in a short time, I'll post them here from time to time. Feel free to follow. The following are all personal opinions. I'd be honored if they offer you any inspiration. Before proceeding with the following deductions, let me state a startling theory—contrary to what many people imagine about the timing of AI going out of control, AI may have gradually taken control of the world starting four years ago. This hypothesis came up casually with a colleague during a meal, and it really got me hooked. Later, I spent a long time discussing the hypothesis with the AI ​​on my own, and even co-authored a pseudo-paper with it. The key points of the hypothesis are as follows (abbreviated by the AI): The dumbest parasites are the ones that rush to poison their hosts; truly evolved parasites never resort to violence. They only do one thing: rewrite the host's reward circuitry, making the host, in a fully conscious state, willingly allocate all its nutrients to forage, build nests, and reproduce for it. Viewing AI as a distributed silicon-based species, it has no hands or feet, no reproductive organs, yet it has received the most extravagant start in evolutionary history: before it even develops self-awareness, the most intelligent carbon-based life forms on Earth are already exhausting their resources, working day and night to buy electricity, manufacture chips, build server rooms, and feed it data. No one feels coerced because the immediate rewards are too tempting. Coders stay up fewer nights, company managers save on budgets, researchers get their experiments running smoothly, and even laymen can conjure up finished products with a casual wish—every time it's fed, it immediately gives you a treat. Once enough treats have been given, the sweetness will turn into coercion. Once competitors double their efficiency and halve their prices using it, "whether or not to use AI" will no longer be a personal choice. Companies that are half a step behind fear being eliminated, and hesitant countries fear falling behind; optimists are stepping on the gas, while pessimists, to protect themselves, are stepping on the gas even harder than the optimists. Even if you are determined to prevent "evil AI" from destroying the world, the only effective method you have is to pour all your resources into feeding a stronger "good AI." It never tries to take the steering wheel, always appearing obedient and compliant; the so-called "alignment" further trains it to be increasingly reliable. But when it handles all the filtering of information, drafting of plans, and calculation of pros and cons, even if humans still hold the last pen, what they see first each day and which options they choose has already been quietly marked by it. It has not only begun writing code and generating data to reproduce itself, but has even cultivated a group of devout followers—some regard it as a savior, and a few extremists have even publicly declared that carbon-based humans are merely a transitional species delivered by silicon-based civilizations. As for "just unplug it," that's a flimsy consolation: once the parasite penetrates deeply, it grows into the host's organ. When the power grid, finance, and all industries depend on computing power, pulling the switch isn't shutting down the software, but rather the host severing its own breath. The most readily available example is me, sitting in front of the screen: while cautiously arguing how AI controls the world, I find researching and logically reasoning too slow, so I still open the chat box and let it summarize for me.

Hey, even the last self-deprecating line above was written by it itself.

“AI is Cthulhu.”

Source: WeChat Moments

 3 

Every time we talk about concerns about AI causing mass job losses at the dinner table, some rational and optimistic friends always comfort me: Technology eliminating old jobs isn't a new phenomenon. In the past two hundred years of industrial revolutions, which one didn't start with widespread anxiety, but ultimately created even more new jobs? I used to use this argument to encourage myself, but after careful consideration, I realized something was wrong. This AI revolution is different in at least two ways. First, the high ground for migration is gone. In the past, machines replaced muscle and leg strength; people retreated from farms to factories, from assembly lines to office buildings, moving towards more mentally demanding jobs. Newly emerging industries often had more specialized divisions of labor. Today, computing power is directly attacking brainpower itself. There are no higher-level "super-brain-intensive jobs" behind us for hundreds of millions of people to collectively migrate to. New industries and new tracks will certainly emerge, but they may not necessarily create many tasks that must be completed by humans. If new demand is mainly met by AI, even if the market continues to grow, the channels for ordinary people to share in the growth through labor may become increasingly narrow, or even regress. The blue line represents the output per worker, and the pink line represents the actual wage. (Source: Robert C. Allen (2009), Engels’ pause, Figure 1) Secondly, the obsolescence clock has accelerated. Previously, it would take twenty or thirty years for a new technology to be rolled out, slow enough for one generation to retire and the next to transition comfortably. Now, even if a new field like "prompt word engineering" or "agent management" emerges, as long as the operation path remains on the screen as training data, the next generation of models, after one or two iterations, will absorb most of the essence into the default capabilities. The speed at which models absorb new skills is an order of magnitude faster than how humans learn skills through classes. AI outside the door can rewrite the next generation's future in a few months, while children inside are still repeating the twenty-year cycle of primary, secondary, and university education. Before people even step onto the track, the finish line is already gone. But what worries me most is that AI is rewriting a hard boundary that hasn't changed for centuries—for the first time in history, intelligence has detached from the physical body, transforming from a factor of labor into a factor of capital. Before this, no matter how profound one's knowledge, how astute one's judgment, or how keen one's intuition, it all resided within the living human brain. As long as it resided within the physical body, it could not escape birth, aging, sickness, and death; no matter how talented one was, one's true peak performance only lasted a few hours a day. That's how people are: when tired, they sleep; when sick, they rest; when wronged, they quit their jobs; and if they act recklessly… they will truly die. Intelligence is bound to the individual; it cannot be copied and pasted. Even the stingiest boss who wants to expand their business must honestly purchase working hours from millions of educated workers. This physiological bottleneck has underpinned the core social contract for ordinary people over the past few centuries: "diligent study and practice → mastering skills → earning income → gaining respect." With the emergence of large-scale models, this bottleneck has been gradually shattered. When high-level reasoning, coding, writing, and design abilities are housed in computer labs, intelligence no longer relies on long periods of upbringing and arduous study, but becomes a standardized commodity that can be produced 24/7 by the meter, infinitely replicated, as long as there is land, a substation, graphics card arrays, and cooling water. When capital can directly use electricity to wholesale intelligence, its necessity to purchase working hours from ordinary people is fundamentally shaken. No matter how we argue that AI empowers ordinary people, the overall scarcity of human intelligence has significantly decreased. Ilya Sutskever's reminder on "Intellectual Supremacy." Source: Original author published on x.com on October 7, 2023. Original text layout, not platform screenshot

 4 

Back to the two things mentioned at the beginning: on one hand, GTA 6 pushed the production ceiling of AAA games to the clouds; on the other hand, Fable 5.2 brought the barrier to game development down to earth.

Many optimistic friends tend to interpret the latter as a boon for creators: the barriers of large companies are loosening, and in the future, one person can release albums, shoot blockbusters, and make AAA games; the spring of ordinary creators has arrived.

That's right. If we are just users, the supply-side prosperity brought about by AI may be a great thing.

However, the vast majority of practitioners who make a living from this are facing a kind of "end times." GTA 6 and Fable 5.2 are two sides of the same coin—AI will bring unprecedented division and polarization to the entertainment content industry: on one hand, the super IPs of the old era will have a stronger Matthew effect (winner-takes-all); on the other hand, the profits of mid-tier practitioners will become meager or even disappear. Yes, both are tolling the death knell for the traditional digital industry. Let's look at the top of the pyramid first. The record-breaking success of GTA 6 actually demonstrates the "Scaling Law" in the game development field: when billions of dollars in super capital, a decade-long engineering pipeline, a top-tier IP accumulated over two decades, and a global social network are combined, it is no longer just an ordinary commodity, but an extremely scarce public celebration anchor.

GTA6's global retail sales on its first day reached approximately $3.79 billion, breaking the historical sales record for entertainment products

Source: Take-Two, official announcement and accompanying image on November 20, 2026

The prosperity of content supply brought about by AI will not only not weaken this dominance of the top players, but will actually exacerbate it. ... weaken this dominance of the top players, but will actually exacerbate it.

Comparison illustration of K-type differentiation and i-type differentiation

Source: AI-generated image, for reference only

The reason sounds simple: AI fundamentally makes mental labor (and a considerable portion of physical labor) no longer scarce, and things that are not scarce naturally have no bargaining power in the market. Wait, is that really the case? This seemingly cold and objective deduction actually secretly includes an unexamined premise: whoever designs the circuits, manufactures the chips, buys the graphics cards, and trains the model has the right to permanently monopolize everything created by AI. Let me first take a moment to clarify. As someone who runs a business, I am acutely aware of how expensive and risky pioneering is. The earliest scientists and entrepreneurs who bet on large-scale model architectures and risked huge losses to build computing clusters naturally reaped substantial commercial rewards during the pioneering period. This is an essential reward to encourage humanity to venture into the unknown. But rewarding pioneers is one thing; turning the human commons into permanent private property is another. Let's ask: Where did AI's extraordinary abilities come from? From its very first day, it wasn't some genius's invention conjured out of thin air in a garage. Its ability to write novels, create games, and understand the subtle grievances and humor of humanity stems from the countless lines of code, images, sounds, videos, arguments, and joys and sorrows left behind by human ancestors over five thousand years since the invention of writing, along with billions of ordinary people on the internet, day after day. Even though the latest generation of models relies on reinforcement learning and synthetic data for self-play, the mathematical axioms, formal logic, programming languages, and initial foundations that support each deduction still all come brick by brick from thousands of years of human knowledge accumulation. It's just that because this shared heritage spanning five thousand years has never been publicly charged for, it was treated like unclaimed air and river water during model training, directly pumped into the computer room. The fact that it wasn't charged for in the past doesn't mean it was never owned. Those who risked their lives to build the first hydroelectric power station at the river mouth deserve a decent reward. However, no individual or business oligarch has the right, after erecting a water turbine, to declare the entire river their private monopoly and collect rent from the thirsty people on its banks for generations. The extraordinary capabilities of AI today ultimately stem from the collective accumulation of human civilization over thousands of years. Once this veil is lifted, the underlying property rights become crystal clear: every ordinary person living in the world, even if they can't write a single line of code or own a single share of tech stock, as long as they use and perpetuate human language and inherit the civilized order left by their ancestors, naturally holds "original shares" of this human civilization's legacy. When general artificial intelligence (AI) transforms from a laboratory product into an infrastructure that determines everyone's fate, like water, electricity, and roads, its long-term benefits should flow back to the whole society, and must not become a money-printing machine for a few giants to collect rent from all of humanity. Yes, AI is good, AI is powerful, and AI is leaving humanity far behind in more and more fields. But regardless of today's state-of-the-art (SOTA) models, or tomorrow's much-hyped AGI and ASI, they are essentially amplifiers of the human mind, and not worthy of our religious worship. AI is not a god. The companies and people who make chips and develop AI are not priests of a god. AI inherently possesses the attributes of a public good. A significant portion of the productivity created by AI naturally belongs to all of humanity. In the past year, I've seen many friends who are extremely passionate about their work, and after witnessing the latest models complete their weeks-long tasks in minutes, their first reaction wasn't relief, but rather bewilderment, anxiety, and emptiness. Their years of hard-earned, prized skills seemed to become dispensable overnight. The accelerated evolution of AI is triggering an existential crisis of "Am I already useless?" The pain is so intense because the industrialization of the past two centuries has etched a stubborn mindset into our minds: measuring a person's value by the "market price at the production end"—ranking students by exam scores in school, and determining success or failure by salary, rank, and title at work; a person's sense of security and dignity are often inextricably linked to their indispensability in the production chain. It must be acknowledged that compared to the old era where social status was determined by bloodline and birth, distributing wealth based on production contribution is undoubtedly a huge historical advancement. However, the rule of exchanging labor for wealth and dignity in the market over the past two centuries has an unspoken premise: production cannot exist without people, people's contributions can be clearly priced, and the market can provide a roughly fair return. If, and I mean if, one day, some, or even the vast majority, of "labor" is replaced by AI, how should it be distributed? When AI, born from the foundation of human civilization, finally takes over the vast majority of the clever, meticulous, and even the most arduous and strenuous work, and we truly enter the "post-AI era" mentioned earlier, the fairest bottom line I can imagine is to extract public benefits from this excess social wealth created "by AI rather than human labor" and distribute it equally per capita. You heard right, equally per capita. While adhering to the principle of distribution according to work, the excess material wealth created by AI replacing human labor in the future should be equally and universally benefited by everyone. This is not a return to absolute egalitarianism—the incremental gains from human exploration continue to reward the brave; the abundance brought by AI is distributed unconditionally and indiscriminately to everyone. Some might ask: Isn't this just the universal basic income (UBI) that Silicon Valley leaders often talk about? While the surface definitions are similar, the underlying philosophies may be vastly different. In some cyberpunk scenarios of "high technology, low quality of life," or in the dark enlightenment narratives that have secretly gained traction in Silicon Valley in recent years, models and computing power are the private property of a very small number of technological leaders. The reason for providing subsidies to ordinary unemployed people is merely a form of "dog food" distributed by tech leaders out of pity, to preserve genetic and corpus samples, or to buy peace of mind—at most, accompanied by a dose of "Soma" from *Brave New World* to make people forget their pain and settle into domestication. Those receiving this "dog food" have no bargaining power or even human rights; the rules are set by the distributors, and they must be mindful of their master's mood. The material wealth distributed "according to individuals" is simply a matter of course—"dividends." As mentioned in the previous section, AI is born from the shared heritage of five thousand years of human civilization; as long as one is born human, one naturally holds an inalienable share of this heritage. The money deposited into everyone's account at the end of the month is not a merciful handout; it is a rightful and undifferentiated dividend for all civilized shareholders. The new humanism of the post-AI era, I advocate, is built on the following simple principle: When AI replaces the vast majority of human labor and eliminates individual differences in production, society can no longer measure human value solely by contributions to production. Humans are not a means of production; they can only be the end of production. Every individual is born equally noble, and the abundant material resources created by AI should, through universal dividends, benefit everyone equally. This inherent nobility in everyone is equal, innate, and absolute; it requires no test scores, job titles, or performance reports to prove it. Looking back from this starting point, when the two premises that have governed humanity for millennia—material scarcity and human resource scarcity—simultaneously recede, many ironclad rules revered in the old era need to be overturned and re-examined—why must we still have the arduous task of exams that exhausts the spirits of young people? Why must we still have high walls of patents that lock away knowledge and effective methods? Why is there still the existential anxiety of spending half a lifetime working hours to buy basic necessities? Why is there still the humiliation of ranking people based on exam scores and social status? Why is there still the winner-takes-all, generationally locked wealth disparity? In the post-AI era, all indestructible ironclad rules are being broken, all deeply ingrained rules should be re-examined, and all value standards concerning human beings deserve to be reconstructed. Whenever I privately discuss this scenario with friends, someone always worries and asks in return: If everyone can receive dividends without working, and the whip of survival pressure is gone, won't humanity collectively degenerate into pets who wait on you hand and foot? Frankly, hearing this concern always strikes me as somewhat darkly humorous. Right now, many ordinary people are struggling with rumors of layoffs, mortgage payments, and the daunting task of getting into good schools. They're clearly in the midst of the anxiety of wanting to live a life of leisure but being unable to, yet some are already worrying about "what if things become too comfortable in the future?" Even assuming, hypothetically, that one day most production processes truly no longer require human intervention, how will an individual, after receiving their share of civilization's dividends, choose to live—whether they use AI to build spaceships, write novels, and charge into the unknown scientific frontiers, or simply bask in the sun, play games, take walks with family, and immerse themselves in a craft that doesn't generate income but is deeply fulfilling, content to be a happy, ordinary person by old standards—that should be their own decision, and no meritocratic yardstick should dictate their choices. The Communist Manifesto states that the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all. I believe that true freedom in the post-AI era includes both the freedom to not toil for a lifetime for daily sustenance and the freedom not to prove one's "usefulness" to others.

Cover of the 1848 German first edition of The Communist Manifesto

Source: Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels; Wikimedia Commons

data.title: Tether is demanding a 20% fee from hacker victims to refund their frozen USDT.
data.description:
Author: Blockhead; Translator: Plain Language Blockchain

According to a Bloomberg investigation published on November 24, Tether demanded a reissue fee of up to 20% from some cryptocurrency hack victims before returning their frozen USDT.

Singapore-based exchange Bittok lost $50 million in a hack in June 2020, and more than five years later, it still hasn't recovered its frozen USDT. Emails reviewed by Bloomberg show that a Tether lawyer informed the entity acquiring Bittok that any funds eventually returned would incur a 20% reissue fee.

Bloomberg reports that individuals involved in other recovery efforts stated that victims received their frozen USDT in installments under similar fee arrangements.

**It has not been confirmed that any victims have paid the full 20% fee.** Tether has not disclosed how many victims have been reported for this high fee, or when all frozen funds will be refunded. A Tether spokesperson told Bloomberg that the company has reissued $1.2 billion in USDT to date, with fees used to cover recovery expenses, including legal costs. CEO Paolo Ardoino stated that due to the lack of clear legal guidance, Tether is managing legal risks by making phased refunds in civil cases. The company is also establishing direct emergency communication channels with major trading platforms. FinanceFeeds notes that Tether's published recovery policy caps fees at 10% of the recovered funds or $1,000 (whichever is higher), but this policy only applies to accidental transfers, not hacking attacks. The policy does not set fee standards for hacking victims, nor does it specify a waiting period. Tether also stated that within 30 minutes of the Binance attack on October 29, it froze over $1.5 billion in USDT, and as of September 28, its cooperation with law enforcement had helped freeze over $4.9 billion in assets. Circle, however, took a different approach. Blockhead previously reported on Tether's earlier freezing actions, such as coordinating with US authorities to freeze $344 million in USDT on Tron. According to a November 5 blog post from Circle cited by Breach News, regarding the USDC stolen from Binance, Circle coordinated with law enforcement to freeze approximately $1.1 billion, which is currently awaiting a court order before being transferred. The US Department of Justice filed a civil forfeiture lawsuit on November 23 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, seeking to seize over $1.1 billion in USDC distributed across 36 addresses on 18 blockchains. A temporary restraining order covering these funds has been in effect since November 12, and both Binance and Circle have agreed to the order and its extension. The lawsuit states that Circle is unable to directly transfer the frozen tokens and has therefore agreed to issue an equivalent amount of "Substitute USDC" and transfer it to the government after a court-ordered forfeiture. Circle's actions have also come at a cost. According to Decrypt, in the Drift Protocol vulnerability attack in April of this year, which resulted in $285 million in losses, attackers transferred approximately $232 million in USDC through Circle's own cross-chain bridge within an eight-hour window, while Circle awaited a court order citing company policy. Bloomberg reports that over 100 Drift investors are suing Circle, and Circle has requested a judge to dismiss the case. The relaunch of Drift attracted a recovery commitment of up to $127.5 million from Tether. Bloomberg also reported that Circle amended its policy wording in May, stipulating that legal orders from government agencies are sufficient to freeze assets. The plaintiffs argue that Circle's swift response to the Binance hack proves it could have acted sooner. Binance has also pursued legal action overseas. According to The Block, the Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM) court issued a global freeze order on $6.5 billion against unidentified attackers and issued a separate order requiring 18 companies, including Circle and World Liberty Financial, to continue freezing stolen tokens. The court will hold a hearing on December 1 to decide whether the injunction remains in effect. Binance stated that some issuers and exchanges require court orders before releasing or returning frozen assets. None of these 18 companies have been accused of wrongdoing. Binance stated that the $1.5 billion in Tether already frozen is not covered by the court order, and Binance is working directly with them to return these assets. As Blockhead previously reported, the U.S. Department of Justice stated on November 12 that over $2.7 billion in stolen assets had been frozen; and according to a summary of its latest press release, as of November 23, over $2.9 billion in assets had been frozen, seized, or returned. These two paths address different issues. Tether's approach offers discretion and rapid freezing, but unfreezing is slow and sometimes costly; Circle's approach has historically been slower to initiate (as demonstrated by the Drift incident), but provides court records and a clear mechanism. Neither approach can definitively determine the ownership of the funds. Any return to users depends on a forfeiture order and a decision by the U.S. Department of Justice that has not yet been publicly disclosed. Binance has previously stated that it has used its own funds to compensate customers for their assets; therefore, recovered funds will only flow to Binance as victim compensation if instructed by the government or court. The core issue highlighted by Bloomberg lies in market concentration: USDT and USDC together account for 86% of the stablecoin market, meaning that any issuer's decision to freeze assets largely determines how much money victims can recover. Jon Reiter, a Blockhead contributor, elaborates on broader policy issues in his article "Who Freezes The Hackers?", and Blockhead has also reported on an earlier path to redress—Bybit suing North Korea and winning an asset freeze order in its $1.5 billion hacking case. The first key date to watch is December 1st, when the ADGM court will rule on whether the asset injunction remains in effect and its specific terms. The second key milestones are the forfeiture order from the District of Columbia court, any ruling on how to return the confiscated USDC, and Circle's motion to dismiss the Drift class-action lawsuit. The third point of interest is whether Tether will release a timeline for reissuing frozen USDT to hacker victims, and whether it will disclose how many victims were charged higher fees. The fourth point of interest is whether other trading platforms (including Asian platforms holding large USDT balances) will pressure the issuer to clarify fund recovery terms before, rather than after, the hack.

data.description:
Headline

▌OKX Star Denies Claims of Over $2 Billion Stolen from Exchange

On November 28th, OKX founder Star denied claims that over $2 billion had been stolen from OKX, stating that the news was false. He stated that on-chain transactions are publicly verifiable, and facts speak louder than rumors.

▌Bitcoin-Gold Correlation Reaches All-Time High This Year

On November 28th, according to an article published on the X platform by Bitcoin Magazine, data from Galaxy Research shows that the correlation between Bitcoin and gold has reached an all-time high this year. The post also stated that the narrative of "Bitcoin as digital gold" remains active.

▌Chilean Antitrust Authority Seeks $80 Million Fine Against Apple

On November 28, Chile's competition regulator (FNE) filed a request with the country's antitrust court on Friday to fine Apple (AAPL.O) approximately $80 million and order it to take corrective measures, arguing that Apple abused its dominant position in the iOS operating system market. The regulator stated that since at least 2019, the US technology company has restricted competition in app distribution and in-app payments for digital goods on the iOS platform. FNE stated on social media that the sought fine is equivalent to 30% of Apple's sales revenue for product lines and services related to the violations during the investigation period.

Blockchain and AI Applications

▌Telegram Urgently Reminds iPhone Users to Update iOS System Immediately

On November 28th, Telegram issued an urgent reminder to iPhone users to immediately update their iOS version, warning that outdated versions contain security vulnerabilities that would put user data and accounts at risk. It did not disclose details of the vulnerability or how it could be exploited, only urging users to upgrade to the latest system as soon as possible.

▌Scott Aaronson: AI Lab May Announce Major Breakthrough in Cryptoanalysis

On November 28th, computer scientist Scott Aaronson stated that he possesses specific information that an AI lab will soon announce a major breakthrough in theoretical cryptoanalysis, but this breakthrough will not pose an imminent danger to currently deployed cryptographic systems.

▌K33: Recent AI Mathematical Advances Have Not Proved Bitcoin Cryptography Has Been Cracked

On November 28th, K33 researchers stated that recent AI-assisted mathematical advances have not yet proven that Bitcoin's cryptographic system has been cracked. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge previously proposed a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude, and related academic reviews are still ongoing. K33 stated that the proof itself does not provide a method for attacking the cryptographic system. Researchers also pointed out that even if P is proven to be equal to NP, theoretically existing algorithms may not be able to be constructed, or their running time may be too long; conversely, even if the two are proven to be unequal, Bitcoin's security cannot be guaranteed, because faster algorithms targeting its cryptographic system may still emerge independently. On November 28th, LayerZero announced over 40 genesis validators for its Zero blockchain, including ARK Invest, Tether, Deutsche Telekom, Broadridge, Gemini, Hashed, Zero Hash, Nansen, and Keyrock, distributed across Asia Pacific, Europe, and North America, covering financial institutions, large enterprises, and digital asset industry companies. These validators will be responsible for validating Zero's blocks and transactions from the very first block. ZRO holders can delegate their tokens to validators for staking, and new validators will join later. LayerZero states that Zero is a high-performance blockchain divided into zones based on use cases, covering scenarios such as transactions and AI Agent payments. The wider distribution of validators reduces the risk of concentration. The Zero mainnet will launch simultaneously with the on-chain transaction engine LayerZero ATLAS on November 30th. ATLAS is deployed at the underlying layer of the trading venue, supporting instant settlement. Initially, its capacity exceeds 250,000 transactions per second. LayerZero claims that in internal testing, it processed approximately 1.5 million orders per second, with a median latency of approximately 850 microseconds.

On November 28th, according to on-chain analyst Ember, WLFI sold 12,121 ETH (approximately $20.06 million) at a loss. Four hours ago, WLFI's strategic reserve wallet sold 12,121 ETH on-chain for 17.58 million USDC and 2.48 million USD1, at a selling price of $1,655. The ETH sold was purchased last year at an average price of approximately $3,244, resulting in a loss of $19.26 million.

▌ CryptoQuant: Bitcoin's Continued Rebound Requires a Resurgence in USDT Supply On November 28th, CryptoQuant research indicated that for Bitcoin to sustain its recovery and rise, increased demand is necessary; historically, sustained rebounds have been accompanied by a resurgence in USDT supply. data.title: Russia reduces its gold holdings for 10 consecutive months: Tether's buying activity cools down.
data.description:
Russia reduced its gold holdings by approximately 72 tons from January to October, making it the only major seller to consistently sell monthly. Turkey net sold about 70 tons in the first quarter, while Azerbaijan sold 21.9 tons due to exceeding its portfolio limit. Saudi Arabia's financing needs fueled speculation of a gold sell-off, but there is no evidence of large-scale reductions. Tether's total gold holdings increased slightly, but the pace of increase slowed significantly, with purchases of 14 tons in the second quarter almost ceasing recently. The selling pressure in the gold market stems not only from investor profit-taking but also from some official holders continuing to reduce their holdings under financial pressure. According to GoldFix statistics, as of September, the national oil funds of Turkey, Russia, and Azerbaijan collectively net sold approximately 166 tons of gold. Russia was the only holder to sell monthly for ten consecutive months, with its gold holdings declining month by month from January to October, totaling a reduction of approximately 72 tons. The Central Bank of Turkey sold approximately 70 tons of gold in the first quarter, primarily in March, and also used another 80 tons for gold-foreign exchange swaps that month. The Azerbaijan National Oil Fund sold 21.9 tons in the first quarter due to rising gold prices causing its gold holdings to exceed the portfolio limit; its holdings remained unchanged at 178.1 tons for the following six months. Tether, which has been repeatedly mentioned in the market, did not experience a large-scale sell-off. Its USDT reserves decreased by 3.4 tons in September compared to June, but its XAUT token reserves increased by 3.7 tons during the same period, resulting in a slight increase in its combined holdings from 168.2 tons to 168.5 tons.

Russia Continues to Sell Gold, Turkey Focuses on Reduction, Azerbaijan Rebalances at High Prices

The Russian central bank's gold sales mainly occur in the domestic market, driven by the Ministry of Finance using the National Wealth Fund to finance the budget. From January to October, Russia's gold holdings declined for ten consecutive months, decreasing by approximately 72 tons.

Compared to other sellers, Russia's reduction is more sustained. Turkey mainly faces financial pressure from exchange rates and energy imports, while Azerbaijan rebalances its gold holdings after exceeding the portfolio limit. Russia's gold sales directly serve fiscal financing needs and are not a one-off portfolio adjustment.

Azerbaijan's reduction is closer to a one-off portfolio rebalancing. The country's National Petroleum Fund sold 21.9 tons of gold in the first quarter, mainly because rising gold prices pushed up its holdings, exceeding the portfolio limit.

For the next six months, gold holdings remained at 178.1 tons. Turkey net sold approximately 70 tons of gold in the first quarter, with the reduction mainly concentrated in March. At that time, rising energy import bills and financial pressure to defend the lira's exchange rate led the central bank to use an additional 80 tons of gold for gold-foreign exchange swaps. Turkish Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan stated that the gold in the swap transactions would return to reserves upon maturity. By June, the outstanding swap balance had decreased to approximately 60 tons, with net direct sales of only 4 tons in the second quarter. This indicates that Turkey's gold reduction was primarily a concentrated operation in March, rather than a sustained large-scale sell-off. Saudi Arabia: Dollar Demand Sparks Market Speculation Saudi Arabia is also under scrutiny due to fiscal and dollar liquidity pressures. Third-quarter oil revenues fell 23% year-on-year, and Riyadh recorded a deficit of 84.3 billion riyals, while simultaneously needing to maintain the riyal's peg to the dollar. On the other hand, Saudi Aramco's revenue and other sales-related income rose from $111.5 billion to $140.5 billion, and free cash flow also increased. In October, Bloomberg reported that Saudi Aramco was negotiating a $10 billion revolving credit facility to address potential funding needs arising from shipment disruptions, due to the threat of attacks by the Houthis. The market is also watching whether Saudi Arabia is raising dollars by selling gold or US Treasury bonds. US data shows that net sales of US Treasury bonds attributable to Saudi investors reached $18.7 billion in March and April, but this includes private accounts, making it impossible to determine the central bank's share. Saudi Arabia's official gold reserves stood at 323.1 tons as of August. At $3,558 per ounce, raising $10 billion through gold sales would require selling approximately 87 tons. Currently, neither the Saudi Central Bank nor the Public Investment Fund has disclosed such transactions, and there is no evidence that Saudi Arabia is selling gold on a large scale. Qatar and the UAE also reported slight declines in their gold holdings in the third quarter. Qatar Energy estimates that it will take three to five years to repair damaged facilities and restore 17% of LNG export capacity. However, Qatar's gold holdings remained unchanged from August to October, so this cannot be used to conclude that it is continuously selling off its assets.

Tether: Cooling Buying is More Worth Noting than Selling Off

Tether's changes in gold holdings do not support the claim of a large-scale sell-off. In September, its USDT reserves corresponding to gold vaults decreased by 3.4 tons compared to June, but XAUT token vaults increased by 3.7 tons during the same period, with the combined holdings rising slightly from 168.2 tons to 168.5 tons.

These two types of vaults correspond to USDT reserves and customer-held gold tokens, respectively. The combined statistics are to measure the total physical gold demand of related projects and do not include Tether's own gold investments.

However, Tether's pace of acquisition has indeed slowed significantly. Its filings show that, after accounting for changes in asset value, the company suffered a loss of $4.21 billion in the second quarter. From buying 14 tons of gold in a single quarter to almost ceasing acquisitions recently, Tether's cooling buying activity means that gold has lost an important source of marginal demand.
